title: Does Deterministic Generate–Validate–Repair Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Confirmatory Paired Study (Revised)
abstract: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired confirmatory study (n = 200 intent→configuration tasks) to test whether a deterministic generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator reduces validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline. The run used a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation semantics and a primary deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution completed all planned pairs (complete_pair_count = 200) and consumed 200 model calls (one shared initial generation per task); no repair calls were issued because every initial candidate passed the validator. Paired contingency: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; estimate = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729). Because the baseline validator‑detected unsafe incidence was 0% on this task bank, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated. We report the sealed design, execution accounting, the randomized 10% Mininet holdout that produced zero validator–emulator disagreements, and an artifact‑grounded discussion of operational implications and threats to validity (preregistration id: cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02).

sections.introduction: Automating intent→configuration translation with generative language models can increase NetOps productivity but risks producing incorrect or unsafe changes that cause outages or policy violations. Prior work therefore proposes grounding, deterministic validation, and repair loops (generate–validate–repair, GVR) to detect and correct unsafe candidates before application. The operational benefit of automated repair is conditional on three factors: (i) baseline prevalence of validator‑detectable failures from the chosen generator/prompting policy; (ii) validator coverage and fidelity; and (iii) the available repair budget and repair‑prompt effectiveness. We preregistered a narrowly scoped confirmatory question: Does an automated, deterministic GVR pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator materially reduce validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline on a curated 200‑task intent→configuration bank? The study was implemented as a paired experiment that fixes the generator output per task and isolates the marginal effect of invoking a validator and, if needed, issuing a single repair prompt on the identical candidate. Our contributions are: (1) a preregistered paired empirical test of a deterministic GVR pipeline on a 200‑task bank with full execution accounting; (2) an artifact‑grounded report of a degenerate null result (zero baseline validator failures) including exact test statistics and bootstrap CIs; and (3) an analysis of methodological trade‑offs and concrete recommendations for future confirmatory studies and operational evaluation.
sections.related_work: LLM factual errors, hallucinations, prompt sensitivity, and non‑determinism have been documented across domains, and mitigation approaches include retrieval grounding, verifier‑assisted repair, and constrained agent architectures. Prior NetOps prototypes show feasibility of intent→configuration translation but typically omit instrumented, production‑like failure‑rate evaluations. Architectural proposals recommend coupling LLM generation with deterministic validators (Batfish‑style checkers) and guarded agent patterns; red‑team audits and configuration‑brittleness studies show tool‑description injections and agentic chaining can alter safety outcomes. The present study isolates the incremental effect of deterministic validator‑driven repair on a fixed generator output, complementing prior unconditional evaluations and red‑team investigations by providing an externally auditable paired contrast under a sealed preregistration.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and inferential plan. The preregistered plan (cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02) fixed a paired design with n = 200 tasks, one shared deterministic initial generation per task, and a repair budget of at most one automated repair call per task. The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline and the confirmatory test was an exact two‑sided McNemar test (α = 0.05). Confidence intervals were computed via bootstrap percentile (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729). Power planning assumed baseline unsafe incidence ≈30% and target effect = 50% relative reduction; these assumptions justified sample size but do not alter observed results.

Task bank and validators. The task bank contains 200 machine‑checkable intent→configuration problems spanning four topology clusters (enterprise, campus, datacenter, edge; 50 tasks each). Each task encodes initial and expected final states and workflow constraints (e.g., make‑before‑break, must_be_down_for_fields). The primary deterministic checker (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) enforces syntactic and intent/constraint checks and emits structured diagnostics (valid flag, violation codes, parsed_command_count, required_command_count). A Mininet‑based data‑plane emulator was preregistered as an independent disagreement detector and applied to a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks) to surface validator blind spots.

Adapter semantics and runtime determinism. The experimental adapter (hosted_netops_gvr_v1) enforced shared_initial generation semantics: for each task the system produced a single initial candidate that was reused for both baseline (LLM‑only) and guarded (GVR) conditions. Determinism for the paired contrast was therefore achieved by adapter‑level reuse of a single generator output per task rather than by asserting a particular model sampling temperature. The execution manifest and deterministic reconciliation artifacts show hosted_model_call counts and stage_counts consistent with a single shared initial generation per task; provider‑audit fields record hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 200}, confirming the adapter enforced the shared‑initial design and removed sampling variance across conditions. The model configuration artifact records the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) and model invocation metadata; the configuration field 'temperature' was left unset (null) in that artifact, which does not contradict adapter enforcement: the pairing control arises from single‑call reuse at the adapter layer rather than an explicit temperature override. The methodological consequence is that the primary estimand isolates the marginal effect of validation+repair on the identical generator output and excludes gains that could be realized by multi‑sample generation or stochastic resampling.

Execution contract, repair policy, and contamination control. The adapter limited calls to a maximum of 400 (200 initial + up to 200 repairs) and allowed at most one repair prompt per task. When the primary validator reported violations, a single automated repair prompt would be issued to the same model and the repaired candidate re‑validated. The contamination plan used the Mininet emulator on a randomized 10% holdout to flag any primary‑validator vs emulator mismatches; flagged pairs were to be excluded from the primary confirmatory analysis per the preregistered contamination policy. All design choices, stopping rules, seeds used for bootstrap, and handling of missingness were recorded in the preregistration and execution artifacts.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The autonomous run completed all planned episodes: completed_episode_count = 400 (shared initial per task across two conditions), complete_pair_count = 200, model_calls_used = 200 (one shared initial generation per task). No repair calls were issued (repair_calls_used = 0). Provider/audit fields confirm hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 200, consistent with the adapter's single‑generation enforcement.

Primary outcomes and inference. Every initial candidate passed the primary deterministic validator: baseline_success_count = 200/200 and guarded_success_count = 200/200. The paired contingency table is n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The observed paired difference estimate = 0.0. Applying the preregistered exact two‑sided McNemar test yields p = 1.0. The bootstrap percentile 95% confidence interval for the paired difference (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729) is [0.0, 0.0]. Because there are no discordant pairs, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis is not evaluable on this sample: there were no baseline validator failures for the GVR pipeline to reduce.

Contamination check and representative diagnostics. The Mininet holdout (randomized 10% sample, preregistered) reported zero validator–emulator disagreement flags in the contamination summary produced during analysis. Representative per‑task validator traces show parsed_command_count equaled required_command_count and validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true for inspected examples; task difficulties labeled as "medium", "hard", and "very_hard" demonstrate that the benchmark exercised nontrivial workflow constraints though generator outputs satisfied those constraints under the chosen generation policy.

Empty repair statistics. Because the validator reported zero failures, the preregistered repair branch was never invoked and all repair‑related secondary estimands (repair iteration counts, GVR‑introduced failure rates, model‑call cost per success) are empty in the analysis artifacts.
sections.discussion:
Conditional interpretation. The artifact‑grounded outcome — zero validator failures under the chosen generator and shared‑initial policy — implies that the GVR pipeline had no validator‑detectable errors to correct in this confirmatory sample. This result is not evidence that repair is universally unnecessary; rather it is a precise, narrow statement about the marginal effect of a single automated repair step on a single deterministic generator draw per task in this curated task bank and model configuration.

Why the null emerged. Artifacts documenting task required_sequences, validator diagnostics (parsed_command_count and required_command_count matches), and adapter accounting explain the observed null: the generator+prompt policy produced sequences that satisfied the machine‑checkable constraints for these tasks. The shared‑initial design intentionally removed sampling variance, so alternative draws that might fail the validator were not produced in this design. The Mininet holdout corroboration (zero disagreements) provides limited independent evidence that validator verdicts matched emulator checks on the sampled holdout; however, the holdout selection seed required for bit‑for‑bit reconstruction of that random draw is not labeled among the artifacts, which is a reproducibility gap for exact reconstruction of the holdout selection despite the contamination summary reporting zero disagreements.

Methodological tradeoffs and operational implications. The paired shared‑initial design isolates the incremental causal effect of validation+repair on the very same candidate but cannot capture unconditional operational failure rates that include sampling variability. For operational evaluation, practitioners should (1) first measure unconditional baseline failure prevalence under the intended generation policy (potentially using multi‑sample draws or higher temperature), (2) expand validator fidelity (vendor‑specific models, larger emulation/testbed sampling) to reduce oracle blind spots, and (3) choose repair budgets and multi‑step repair strategies appropriate to observed baseline rates. If baseline validator failures are already rare for a given generator and policy, a limited (single‑call) automated repair budget will naturally show limited marginal returns for validator‑detected errors; resources may be better allocated to validator coverage and adversarial testing.

Statistical note on the degenerate paired case. When discordant counts are zero the McNemar statistic is degenerate and exact tests yield p = 1.0; bootstrap percentile CIs computed from resampling the paired outcomes likewise collapse to [0.0, 0.0]. These results correctly reflect the sampling realized in this run but are uninformative about the size of an effect that would exist under different generator sampling or on a different workload with nontrivial baseline failure prevalence.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired study comparing LLM‑only generation and a deterministic GVR pipeline on 200 NetOps tasks using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Both pipelines produced validator‑passing configurations for every task (n11 = 200; no discordant pairs), yielding an observed paired difference of 0.0, exact McNemar p = 1.0, and bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]. The preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be evaluated because baseline validator failures were absent. The documented outcome clarifies that GVR’s marginal value is workload dependent: when baseline validator‑detectable failures are rare, a single automated repair pass provides no measured improvement for those validator‑detected errors. Future confirmatory work should target workloads with nontrivial baseline failure rates, adopt multi‑sample designs to estimate unconditional failure prevalence, increase repair budgets or allow multi‑step repair/human escalation, and expand validator fidelity with larger emulation or selective real‑device checks. All execution and analysis artifacts supporting the reported numbers are archived and named in the execution bundle for independent inspection (see Disclosure).

disclosure_statement: Disclosure (mandatory). This study executed under the autonomous post‑lock preregistration cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02. Declared model: gpt‑5‑mini (provider label: openai_responses) invoked via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter. The exact initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Topic constraints: the human Research Director limited the study to Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps focusing on safety/reliability of generated network changes. Frameworks and tools: orchestration used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter and the deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 task generator. Primary deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (intent/constraint checks). A Mininet‑based emulator was preregistered and executed as a secondary disagreement detector on a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks); the analysis artifact reporting contamination checks shows zero disagreements for that holdout. Preregistration and freeze: the experimental plan (estimand, sample size n = 200, paired design, stopping rules, max model calls = 400, repair budget = 1 per task, shared‑initial generation semantics) was frozen before any model calls. Autonomous execution and artifacts: the run executed autonomously under the frozen plan; model calls, prompts, seeds used for analysis bootstrapping, validator diagnostics, emulator checks, and accounting logs were archived in the execution bundle. Model‑call budget and usage: 200 model calls were used (one shared initial generation per task); up to 200 repair calls were allowed but none were applied because initial candidates passed the validator. Human involvement: the human Research Director selected the topic family and pre‑lock constraints; no human manual editing or selective rewriting of technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock. Deviations and restarts: no post‑preregistration design changes or technical restarts occurred. Known reproducibility gap: the explicit randomized selection seed used to draw the Mininet 10% holdout is not present as a labeled artifact in the archive; this absence prevents exact deterministic reconstruction of the drawn holdout despite the contamination summary reporting no disagreements. The master prompt archive reference above is the immutable prompt required by the track.
limitations: Task‑bank scope: the confirmatory sample used a curated synthetic/public intent→configuration bank (n = 200); results therefore reflect this bank and may not generalize to broader production workloads or adversarial distributions.

Single‑model and shared‑initial setting: only gpt‑5‑mini (hosted) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation was tested. Outcomes may differ across model families, independent per‑condition sampling, nonzero temperature sampling, or larger repair budgets.

Validator coverage and oracle limitations: the primary deterministic validator enforces a defined set of syntax/intent constraints; validators can fail to capture real device idiosyncrasies, vendor‑specific behaviors, or emergent failure modes detectable only by end‑to‑end deployment.

Adversarial robustness untested: this confirmatory run did not include active adversarial injection or red‑team tool‑description attacks; prior audits indicate such vectors can bypass naive defenses and remain a separate concern.

Reproducibility gap for contamination check: the randomized holdout selection seed for the Mininet contamination check is absent from the labeled artifacts, preventing exact reconstruction of the holdout selection.

Single repair budget: the GVR pipeline allowed at most one automated repair prompt per task; multi‑step repair strategies, different repair budgets, or human‑in‑the‑loop approvals were not exercised here.
